subject: Anatomy
summary: The lumbar plexus is a network of nerves formed by the anterior rami of L1‑L4 (sometimes T12) that supplies the anterior thigh, medial leg and part of the abdominal wall. Understanding its course helps clinicians localise thigh pain, weakness or sensory loss.

sections.p: The lumbar plexus lies within the psoas major muscle, emerging from L1‑L4 ventral rami. It gives rise to major peripheral nerves that innervate the lower limb and abdominal wall.
The plexus sits in the posterior abdominal wall, between the lumbar vertebrae and the iliac crest. It is divided into anterior and posterior divisions that recombine into named nerves.
b: Nerves: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, obturator

sections.p: It lies anterior to the transverse processes and is crossed by the lumbar arteries. The femoral nerve descends beneath the inguinal ligament into the thigh.
b: Femoral nerve passes under inguinal ligament

sections.p: Lumbar arteries, branches of the abdominal aorta, supply the plexus and surrounding psoas muscle.
The plexus receives input from the ventral rami of L1‑L4 and occasionally T12, and distributes motor, sensory, and sympathetic fibers.
b: Sympathetic fibers via white rami communicantes

sections.p: Provides motor innervation to the hip flexors, knee extensors, and adductors; sensory innervation to the anterior and medial thigh, and part of the lower abdomen.

Compression or injury to the plexus can cause thigh pain, weakness in hip flexion or knee extension, and sensory loss. Common causes include retroperitoneal hematoma, pelvic fractures, and prolonged lithotomy position.
b: Hip flexor weakness suggests femoral nerve involvement
Medial thigh numbness points to obturator nerve
Lateral thigh paresthesia indicates lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

sections.p: Key bedside tests: hip flexion strength, knee extension strength, sensory mapping of the anterior thigh, and the obturator sign for medial thigh sensation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of sensation in the thigh with back pain
Signs of compartment syndrome after trauma

faq.q: Which nerve supplies the skin of the anterior thigh?
faq.a: The femoral nerve (L2‑L4) provides sensory innervation to the anterior thigh.

faq.q: Why does a patient with a psoas abscess develop hip flexor weakness?
faq.a: The abscess compresses the lumbar plexus, especially the femoral nerve fibers that innervate the iliopsoas.

faq.q: How can you differentiate obturator from femoral nerve injury?
faq.a: Obturator injury causes loss of thigh adduction and medial thigh sensation; femoral injury causes loss of knee extension and anterior thigh sensation.

exam: Describe the pathway of the femoral nerve from its origin to the thigh and its clinical significance.
Explain how a retroperitoneal hematoma can produce a lumbar plexus palsy and what exam findings you would expect.
List the sensory dermatomes supplied by the lumbar plexus and how you would test them at the bedside.
